summary.text: The proof splits admissible integers by parity: even \(x\) satisfies \(2\varphi(x)\le x\), while for odd \(x\), \(v_2(\varphi(x))\) is the sum of \(v_2(p-1)\) over its prime divisors. A non-Fermat-type prime divisor supplies the needed extra factor of \(2\); if all divisors are Fermat primes, their distinct valuations below level \(33\) sum to at most \(1+2+\cdots+2^{32}=2^{33}-1\), so one must occur at or above the target level, with equality ruled out in the composite case.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N=2^{33},\qquad F=F_{33}=2^N+1,
\]
and define
\[
a(N)=\min\{m\ge 1:2^N\mid \varphi(m)\}.
\]
We prove that
\[
a(N)=\begin{cases}
F,&F\text{ is prime},\\
2^{N+1},&F\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]
The proof consists of several elementary bounds, followed by the two cases concerning the primality of \(F\).

Throughout, for a positive integer \(r\), write \(\nu _2(r)\) for the exponent of \(2\) in the prime factorization of \(r\). Thus
\[
2^e\mid r\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad e\le \nu _2(r).
\]

### 1. Two elementary facts about primes of the form \(2^s+1\)

We first prove that if \(s\ge 1\) and \(2^s+1\) is prime, then \(s\) is a power of two.

Write
\[
s=2^k u,
\]
where \(u\) is odd. If \(u>1\), then in fact \(u\ge 3\). Put \(z=2^{2^k}\). Since \(u\) is odd, the standard factorization of a sum of odd powers gives
\[
z+1\mid z^u+1.
\]
But
\[
z^u+1=2^{2^ku}+1=2^s+1.
\]
Moreover, when \(u\ge 3\),
\[
1<z+1<z^u+1.
\]
Thus \(2^s+1\) would have a proper nontrivial divisor, contrary to primality. Hence \(u=1\), so \(s=2^k\).

We will also need a quantitative distinction between primes of the form \(2^s+1\) and all other primes. Let \(p\) be prime, put
\[
t=\nu _2(p-1),
\]
and suppose that \(p\) is not of the form \(2^s+1\). Write
\[
p-1=2^t u
\]
with \(u\) odd. If \(u=1\), then \(p=2^t+1\), contrary to the assumption. Therefore \(u\ge 3\), and hence
\[
p=2^t u+1\ge 3\cdot 2^t+1>2^{t+1}.
\tag{1}
\]
For every prime \(p\), whether Fermat-type or not, we also have the weaker bound
\[
2^{\nu _2(p-1)}\le p-1<p.
\tag{2}
\]

### 2. A product dichotomy for a finite set of primes

Let \(T\) be a finite set of primes, and set
\[
S(T)=\sum_{p\in T}\nu _2(p-1).
\]
We claim that one of the following alternatives holds:

1. \(\displaystyle \prod_{p\in T}p\ge 2^{1+S(T)}\); or
2. every \(p\in T\) has the form \(p=2^s+1\).

Indeed, if every member of \(T\) has that form, the second alternative holds. Otherwise choose a member \(q\in T\) which is not of that form. By (1),
\[
q>2^{\nu _2(q-1)+1}.
\]
For every other \(p\in T\), (2) gives
\[
p\ge 2^{\nu _2(p-1)}.
\]
Multiplying these inequalities yields
\[
\prod_{p\in T}p
\ge 2^{\nu _2(q-1)+1}
   \prod_{\substack{p\in T\\p\ne q}}2^{\nu _2(p-1)}
=2^{1+S(T)}.
\]
This proves the dichotomy.

### 3. The \(2\)-adic valuation of the totient of an odd integer

Suppose that \(x\) is odd and has prime factorization
\[
x=\prod_{p\mid x}p^{e_p}.
\]
Euler's product formula gives
\[
\varphi(x)=\prod_{p\mid x}p^{e_p-1}(p-1).
\]
Every prime divisor \(p\) of the odd integer \(x\) is odd. Consequently each factor \(p^{e_p-1}\) is odd and contributes nothing to the \(2\)-adic valuation. Valuations add over products, so
\[
\nu _2(\varphi(x))=
\sum_{p\mid x}\nu _2(p-1),
\tag{3}
\]
where the sum runs over the distinct prime divisors of \(x\).

We also recall that the radical of \(x\) divides \(x\):
\[
\prod_{p\mid x}p\mid x.
\]
For positive \(x\), this implies
\[
\prod_{p\mid x}p\le x.
\tag{4}
\]

### 4. The exceptional Fermat-prime counting argument

We next establish the fact that makes the special index \(N=2^{33}\) work.

Let \(T\) be a finite set of odd primes, every one of which has the form
\[
p=2^s+1.
\]
Suppose
\[
\sum_{p\in T}\nu _2(p-1)\ge 2^{33}.
\tag{5}
\]
Then some \(p\in T\) satisfies
\[
\nu _2(p-1)\ge 2^{33}.
\tag{6}
\]

To prove this, suppose instead that every term is less than \(2^{33}\). For a given \(p=2^s+1\), we have
\[
\nu _2(p-1)=\nu _2(2^s)=s.
\tag{7}
\]
The case \(s=0\) would give \(p=2\), which is excluded because the primes in \(T\) are odd. Thus \(s\ge1\). Since \(p=2^s+1\) is prime, the first fact from Section 1 shows that
\[
s=2^k
\]
for some \(k\ge0\). Our supposition \(s<2^{33}\) then forces \(k<33\).

Furthermore, two distinct primes in \(T\) cannot give the same value of \(s\), because \(p=2^s+1\) uniquely determines \(p\). Hence the distinct numbers \(\nu _2(p-1)\), as \(p\) ranges over \(T\), form a subset of
\[
\{2^0,2^1,\ldots,2^{32}\}.
\]
Their sum is therefore at most
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{32}2^k=2^{33}-1,
\]
contradicting (5). Thus (6) follows.

Notice that this argument does not assume that any particular Fermat numbers below \(F_{33}\) are prime. It merely bounds the possible distinct exponents of those Fermat-type numbers which happen to be prime.

### 5. Two general lower bounds for admissible integers

Call a positive integer \(x\) admissible if
\[
2^N\mid\varphi(x).
\]
First, every admissible \(x\) satisfies
\[
x\ge 2^N+1.
\tag{8}
\]
Indeed, \(x\ne1\), since \(\varphi(1)=1\) and \(N\ge1\), so \(2^N\nmid1\). Thus \(x>1\). For every integer \(x>1\), \(\varphi(x)<x\). On the other hand, divisibility and positivity give
\[
2^N\le\varphi(x).
\]
Therefore
\[
2^N\le\varphi(x)<x,
\]
which, since these are integers, implies (8).

We now prove the stronger bound needed when \(F=2^N+1\) is not prime:
\[
2^{N+1}\le x
\quad\text{for every admissible }x.
\tag{9}
\]

We split according as \(x\) is even or odd.

#### Even case

For every positive even integer \(x\),
\[
2\varphi(x)\le x.
\tag{10}
\]
To see this, write
\[
x=2^a b,
\]
where \(a\ge1\) and \(b\) is odd. Since \(2^a\) and \(b\) are coprime,
\[
\varphi(x)=\varphi(2^a)\varphi(b)=2^{a-1}\varphi(b).
\]
As \(\varphi(b)\le b\), it follows that
\[
2\varphi(x)=2^a\varphi(b)\le2^ab=x.
\]
If \(x\) is admissible, then \(\varphi(x)\ge2^N\), so (10) gives
\[
x\ge2\varphi(x)\ge2^{N+1}.
\]
This proves (9) for even \(x\).

#### Odd case

Now suppose that \(x\) is odd, and let \(T\) be the set of its distinct prime divisors. Since \(2^N\mid\varphi(x)\),
\[
N\le\nu _2(\varphi(x)).
\]
Using (3), this becomes
\[
N\le S(T):=\sum_{p\in T}\nu _2(p-1).
\tag{11}
\]
Apply the product dichotomy of Section 2.

If its first alternative holds, then by (11),
\[
2^{N+1}\le2^{1+S(T)}
\le\prod_{p\in T}p.
\]
Together with (4), this gives
\[
2^{N+1}\le x,
\]
as required.

It remains to consider the second alternative, in which every prime divisor \(p\) of \(x\) is of the form \(2^s+1\). All these primes are odd because \(x\) is odd. Since \(N=2^{33}\), inequality (11) and the counting argument of Section 4 show that there is some prime divisor \(p\mid x\) such that
\[
\nu _2(p-1)\ge 2^{33}=N.
\]
Write \(p=2^s+1\). By (7), \(s=\nu _2(p-1)\), so
\[
s\ge N.
\tag{12}
\]
There are now two integer cases.

If \(s<N+1\), then (12) forces \(s=N\). Hence
\[
p=2^N+1=F.
\]
But \(p\) is a prime divisor of \(x\), so \(p\) is prime, contradicting the present assumption that \(F\) is not prime.

The only remaining possibility is
\[
s\ge N+1.
\]
Then
\[
2^{N+1}\le2^s<2^s+1=p.
\]
Since \(p\mid x\) and \(x>0\), we have \(p\le x\), and consequently
\[
2^{N+1}\le x.
\]
This completes the odd case and proves the stronger lower bound (9) whenever \(F\) is not prime.

### 6. Determination of the minimum

We can now determine the least admissible integer.

Suppose first that \(F=2^N+1\) is prime. Then
\[
\varphi(F)=F-1=2^N,
\]
so \(F\) is admissible. Conversely, the general lower bound (8) says that every admissible positive integer \(x\) satisfies
\[
x\ge2^N+1=F.
\]
Thus \(F\) is exactly the least admissible integer, and
\[
a(N)=F.
\]

Now suppose that \(F\) is not prime. The integer
\[
y=2^{N+1}
\]
is admissible, because the totient of a positive power of two is
\[
\varphi(2^{N+1})=2^N,
\]
which is divisible by \(2^N\). On the other hand, the stronger lower bound (9) says that every admissible positive integer \(x\) satisfies
\[
x\ge2^{N+1}=y.
\]
Therefore \(y\) is the least admissible integer, and
\[
a(N)=2^{N+1}.
\]

Finally, substituting \(N=2^{33}\) and \(F=F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1\) yields
\[
\boxed{
 a(2^{33})=
 \begin{cases}
 F_{33},&F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\[2mm]
 2^{2^{33}+1},&F_{33}\text{ is not prime}.
 \end{cases}}
\]
which is the claimed result.
